answers.answer: Fifty boxes of earth, all shipped from Varna in the Demeter and delivered to the old chapel at Carfax. By 1 October at least 21 had been removed; Harker traced nine great boxes from Carfax to a house in Piccadilly. Other boxes were taken to Bermondsey and Mile End, which the group planned to search.

First mentioned on 26 July 1893 by Mina Murray in her journal: Lucy 'has lately taken to her old habit of walking in her sleep', and Mrs Westenra asked Mina to lock their door at night. Mina's journal of 8 August is the first scene of Lucy actually sleepwalking.

Of Lucy's nine entries (eight letters and diary entries plus one memorandum), only her diary entry of 12 September 1893 (e0106) never mentions Arthur. The other eight do, including the memorandum of 17 September, which ends 'Good-bye, dear Arthur'.

Four transfusions, in order: (1) 7 September, Arthur Holmwood, operated by Van Helsing; (2) 10 September, Dr Seward; (3) 13 September, Van Helsing donated and Seward operated; (4) 18 September, Quincey Morris, after Van Helsing said 'A brave man's blood is the best thing on this earth'. Van Helsing later remarks that Lucy had 'the blood of four strong men'.

The garlic came from Haarlem, from Van Helsing's friend Vanderpool, who grew the herb in his glass-houses; a boxful arrived daily. Van Helsing arranged it: he brought the big parcel himself, made the wreath for Lucy's neck, and with Seward decked the room and placed the flowers and the garlic at her window and door.

First appears on 5 May 1893 in Jonathan Harker's journal in an entry written at the Castle, recalling the coach-yard in Bistritz, where he looked up the Slovak and Servian words 'vrolok' and 'vlkoslak', which he glossed as 'either were-wolf or vampire'. He noted he must ask the Count about the superstitions.

One document: a letter of 25 May 1893 from Quincey P. Morris to the Hon. Arthur Holmwood ('My dear Art'), inviting him to a camp-fire the next night with Jack Seward, signed 'QUINCEY P. MORRIS'. No other passage in the store is from Morris's own hand; all other mentions report his speech or actions.

experience:
The first search was a poor guide: the ranked results mixed relevant passages with unrelated ones (a Harker journal about the train and an unrelated Mina entry), so I used grep for exact words almost every time. grep was the workhorse. Its header ('70 passages match (41 entries)') told me how big a question was before I read anything, and 'raise --limit' with 'N more not shown' was clear. Matching a word start made 'Art' useful for Arthur, though it also gave noise.

What misled me: 'list --source Lucy --without Arthur --by-entry' printed all nine entries as if the filter had not applied, while 'grep --by-entry' gave eight. I had to work out the answer from the grep and then check passage e0106.1 by hand. 'read' and 'around' take passage ids such as e0106.1, but when I gave an entry id (e0106) they crashed with a Python KeyError traceback and no hint. The 'task' command said only 'the walk log is empty', so I could not tell what it tracked. I wished the list filter had worked on entries, that entry ids were accepted by read and around, and that --by-entry said which passages decided the match.
